original_question: Find a more natural mechanism for energy dissipation in the proposed infinite mechanical cascade model that does not rely on inserting explicit friction by hand.
target_in_paper: Problem 39 in Section 15.2 ("A model of energy equidistribution"): "Is there a more natural way to introduce energy dissipation without explicit introduction of a friction mechanism?"
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the core intent of the paper's open problem: the authors want an intrinsic explanation of energy dissipation in their infinite mechanical model, and they explicitly reject solving it by simply adding friction by hand.
missing_details: The relevant setting is specifically the Section 15.2 countable Hamiltonian ball model inside a bounded domain D, not the later inverse-cascade chamber model of Section 15.3.
The system is partitioned into families F1, F2, ..., where family Fi contains ni identical balls of radius ri and mass mi.

The phase variables are the positions qj and momenta pj of the balls, and the dynamics are given by the Hamiltonian H(p,q)=Σ_i Σ_{Bj in Fi} pj^2/(2mi) + Σ_i Σ_{Bj in Fi, Bk in F_{i+1}} U_{i,i+1}(|qj-qk|).
A paper-critical assumption is that balls in family Fi interact only with the neighboring families Fi-1 and Fi+1, while they pass through balls from all other families without resistance.
The total mass condition Σ_i ni mi < infinity and the assumption that mi and ri decrease sufficiently fast are part of the model context that your draft leaves implicit.

Problem 39 is asked only after the preceding conditional question of whether one can choose ni, mi, ri so that a direct energy cascade toward larger family index i occurs and energy escapes from the system.
The specific workaround being excluded is the paper's "limit absorption principle": add friction to the balls in family FN and then let N tend to infinity; the authors call this circular.
The nearby Duchon-Robert sentence is presented as an additional possible connection to weak Euler dissipation, not as an equivalent restatement of Problem 39.

No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree restriction, nilpotency condition, or phrase of the form "for all sufficiently large m" is involved here; those notions are not applicable to this mechanical-dynamical problem.
refined_question: In the Section 15.2 countable Hamiltonian model of balls moving in a bounded box D, with families F1, F2, ... such that family Fi contains ni identical balls of radius ri and mass mi, only neighboring families interact through pair potentials U_{i,i+1}(|qj-qk|), and Σ_i ni mi < infinity with mi and ri decreasing sufficiently fast, suppose these parameters can be chosen so that a direct energy cascade transports energy toward larger family index i and lets energy escape to infinity. Can one then give an intrinsic, non-circular mechanism for this energy dissipation that does not use the ad hoc "limit absorption" device of inserting friction on family FN and then sending N to infinity?
justification: The draft is very close to the paper's actual target and is best matched to Problem 39 in Section 15.2. The key refinements needed for a stand-alone version are to identify the exact model (the countable-family Hamiltonian gas of balls), to indicate that the dissipation question arises after the preceding direct-cascade question, and to specify the precise excluded workaround: friction added to the Nth family and then pushed to infinity. The sentence after Problem 39 about Duchon-Robert dissipation is only an additional suggested connection, so it should not replace the official problem statement. Because the draft clearly points to the cascade section, there is no reason to redirect it to any earlier proposition or theorem.
